options: SageMaker Inference Recommender, which runs load tests across candidate instance types and returns latency, throughput, and cost recommendations
SageMaker Model Monitor with a custom latency baseline
SageMaker Clarify bias and explainability reports
SageMaker Debugger profiling rules
explanation: Inference Recommender automates load testing across instance types and configurations and reports latency, throughput, and cost so you can pick a configuration that meets an SLA without manual benchmarking. Model Monitor watches data/quality drift, Clarify handles bias/explainability, and Debugger profiles training, none of which size inference endpoints.

question: A team is moving a real-time LLM endpoint to a scale-to-zero autoscaling configuration to cut idle GPU cost. Which considerations are valid trade-offs or requirements they must account for? (Select TWO.)
options: The first request after scaling in to zero will incur a cold-start delay while a new instance and model are provisioned
They should configure a step or target-tracking scaling policy plus an appropriate cooldown to avoid thrashing on bursty traffic
Scale to zero removes the need to choose an instance type for the endpoint
Scale to zero converts the endpoint to Serverless Inference automatically
Latency-sensitive synchronous traffic with no tolerance for cold starts is an ideal fit for scale to zero
explanation: Scaling in to zero saves cost but means the first request after idle pays a cold-start penalty, and you still tune scaling policies and cooldowns so bursty traffic does not cause rapid scale in/out thrash. You still select an instance type, the endpoint remains real-time (not converted to Serverless), and strictly latency-sensitive traffic that cannot tolerate cold starts is a poor fit.

question: A regulated bank wants to fine-tune an open-weights 8B model on sensitive proprietary data, keep full control of the weights, and host it in their own VPC with no data leaving their account boundary. They have an ML platform team. Bedrock or SageMaker?
options: SageMaker: fine-tune via JumpStart/training jobs and host on a VPC-attached endpoint, retaining the model artifacts in their own S3
Bedrock on-demand with a system prompt that instructs the model to follow bank policies
Bedrock with Provisioned Throughput for any base FM and no fine-tuning
A third-party hosted API gated behind a firewall rule
explanation: SageMaker lets the bank fine-tune open weights, keep the resulting artifacts in their own account, and deploy to a VPC-isolated endpoint, satisfying control and data-residency requirements. Bedrock abstracts away weight ownership and not all FMs are customizable; a system prompt does not provide weight control or true data isolation, and a third-party API moves data outside the account.

question: A model owner deploys a 34B code model with the LMI container on a single ml.g5.48xlarge (8x A10G, 192 GB GPU memory total). Generation throughput is far below expectations and GPU utilization is low. Inspecting the config, tensor_parallel_degree is set to 1. What is the BEST fix?
options: Increase tensor_parallel_degree to 8 so the model is sharded across all eight GPUs and utilizes the full instance
Reduce the batch size to 1 to lower memory pressure
Switch to a CPU instance to avoid GPU contention
Disable continuous batching to simplify scheduling
explanation: With tensor_parallel_degree=1 the LMI container loads the model on a single GPU and ignores the other seven, causing low aggregate utilization and throughput; setting it to 8 shards the model across all GPUs of the instance. Reducing batch size, moving to CPU, or disabling continuous batching would all further hurt throughput.

question: A product has predictable, steady production traffic for a 7B model 24/7 and wants to reduce hosting cost below standard on-demand SageMaker hosting pricing, while keeping the same managed endpoint. Which option is the BEST cost lever?
options: Purchase a SageMaker Savings Plan committing to a consistent hourly compute spend for a 1- or 3-year term
Move the workload to Serverless Inference to pay only per request
Enable scale to zero so the endpoint is free overnight
Switch to Asynchronous Inference to batch the steady traffic
explanation: For steady, always-on usage, a SageMaker Savings Plan provides the deepest discount on hosting compute in exchange for a term commitment, directly lowering cost without changing the architecture. Serverless cannot host a 7B GPU model and is not cheaper at sustained high utilization, scale to zero gives no benefit on 24/7 traffic, and Async does not reduce per-hour instance cost for steady demand.

question: An architect is choosing between Amazon Bedrock and self-hosting on SageMaker for a new generative feature. Which factors specifically favor choosing SageMaker over Bedrock? (Select TWO.)
options: The required base model is an open-weights model not offered in the Bedrock catalog and must be heavily customized
The team needs fine-grained control over inference server internals such as LMI batching, tensor parallelism, and quantization
They want zero infrastructure management and per-token billing with no idle cost
They need built-in, fully managed Guardrails with no custom container work
They want the fastest possible time-to-first-prototype with no ML ops staff
explanation: SageMaker is favored when you must host an open-weights model outside Bedrock's catalog and when you need low-level control of the serving stack (LMI batching, tensor parallelism, quantization). Zero infra management, per-token billing, managed Guardrails, and fastest no-ops prototyping all favor Bedrock instead.

question: A team serves a fine-tuned 7B model and wants to A/B test a new fine-tune against the current production model on live traffic, gradually shifting traffic and rolling back instantly if quality drops, all behind a single endpoint URL. Which SageMaker feature is the BEST fit?
options: Two production variants on one endpoint with weighted traffic splitting that can be adjusted or rolled back without changing the client
Two separate endpoints with a client-side coin flip to route traffic
A Multi-Model Endpoint loading both variants by model name
Shadow testing with the new variant receiving 100% of traffic
explanation: Production variants on a single endpoint let you assign and dynamically adjust traffic weights for A/B testing and instantly shift back to the stable variant, all transparent to the client. Client-side routing pushes logic to callers, Multi-Model Endpoints are for many distinct models rather than weighted experiments, and a shadow test does not serve a controlled live split.

question: A real-time LLM endpoint must autoscale on signals that reflect actual GPU saturation rather than CPU or simple request count, because invocations vary widely in token length. Which autoscaling choices are appropriate? (Select TWO.)
options: Target-tracking on a per-copy concurrent-requests metric that correlates with GPU load
Target-tracking on a custom CloudWatch GPU-utilization metric emitted by the container
Target-tracking on CPUUtilization of the hosting instances
A fixed scheduled scaling action that adds one instance every hour regardless of load
Scaling on the endpoint's InvocationsPerInstance count alone, ignoring concurrency
explanation: For GPU LLM serving, scaling on a per-copy concurrent-requests metric or a custom GPU-utilization metric tracks real saturation, since both correlate with GPU load under variable token lengths. Raw CPUUtilization is a poor proxy, scheduled-only scaling cannot react to demand, and invocation count alone misses long-running requests.

question: A company wants to quickly evaluate and deploy a popular open-weights LLM with a pre-validated, optimized serving container and a one-click deploy, while still retaining the option to fine-tune it later on their own data. Which SageMaker capability is the BEST starting point?
options: SageMaker JumpStart, which offers curated foundation models with pre-built deploy and fine-tune workflows and optimized containers
Building a custom Docker container from scratch and registering it in ECR
Amazon Bedrock custom model import only
SageMaker Canvas no-code predictions
explanation: JumpStart provides curated foundation models with one-click deployment using optimized containers and built-in fine-tuning recipes, giving the fastest validated path that still supports later customization. Building a container from scratch is slow, Bedrock custom import is a different managed path without JumpStart's catalog/fine-tune UX, and Canvas targets no-code tabular/AutoML use cases.

question: An LMI deployment of a 13B model on inf2 (Inferentia2) is being prepared. Which statements about serving on Inferentia2 are correct considerations? (Select TWO.)
options: The model must be compiled to Neuron format (via the Neuron SDK / Optimum Neuron or AOT compilation) before or at endpoint startup
Inferentia2 is generally chosen for cost-efficient, high-throughput inference rather than as a training accelerator
Inferentia2 instances run unmodified CUDA kernels with no compilation step
Inferentia2 cannot be used with the LMI container and requires a fully custom container
Trainium (trn1) is the recommended choice over inf2 specifically to minimize inference cost
explanation: Models must be compiled to the Neuron format to run on Inferentia2, which is purpose-built for cost-efficient, high-throughput inference. Inferentia2 does not run CUDA kernels, it is supported by LMI/Neuron DLCs (not a mandatory fully custom container), and Trainium is optimized for training, not minimizing inference cost.

question: A 7B model endpoint experiences brief but sharp traffic spikes a few times per day; standard instance autoscaling cannot launch GPU instances fast enough to absorb the spike, causing throttling. The team wants to react to spikes faster than instance launch time. Which approach BEST mitigates this within SageMaker hosting?
options: Use Inference Components and scale the number of model copies/components, combined with provisioned headroom, to absorb spikes faster than full instance scale-out
Set the autoscaling cooldown to several minutes to smooth the spikes
Reduce the minimum instance count to zero to save money during the spikes
Switch the endpoint to Batch Transform during spike windows
explanation: Inference Components allow scaling at the model-copy level on already-provisioned compute and maintaining headroom, reacting faster than waiting for new GPU instances to launch. A long cooldown delays reaction, scaling to zero worsens cold-start during spikes, and Batch Transform is offline and cannot serve real-time spike traffic.

question: A team needs to host a 175B-parameter model that exceeds the GPU memory of any single instance type. They want a managed SageMaker path that shards the model across multiple GPUs within the largest available instance and uses an optimized inference engine. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?
options: LMI container with a high tensor_parallel_degree on a p4d/p4de/p5-class instance, using an optimized backend such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM
Serverless Inference with the maximum 6 GB memory setting
A Multi-Model Endpoint loading shards as separate models on demand
A single ml.g5.2xlarge with 8-bit quantization
explanation: A 175B model requires sharding across many high-memory GPUs, which the LMI container does via tensor parallelism on p4d/p4de/p5-class instances with optimized engines like vLLM or TensorRT-LLM. Serverless caps at small CPU/memory, Multi-Model Endpoints do not shard one model across GPUs, and a single g5.2xlarge has nowhere near enough memory even quantized.

question: A developer wants the simplest serverless-style hosting for a small generative text-classification model (under 4 GB, CPU-capable) with unpredictable, infrequent traffic and no desire to manage instances or pay for idle time. The model does not require a GPU. Which option fits BEST?
options: SageMaker Serverless Inference, which auto-provisions compute per request and charges only for usage with no idle cost
A real-time endpoint on ml.g5.xlarge with scale to zero
Asynchronous Inference on a p4d instance
Batch Transform triggered on a 1-minute schedule
explanation: Serverless Inference is ideal for small, CPU-friendly models with intermittent traffic: it scales compute per request and charges only for actual usage with no idle cost or instance management. A GPU real-time endpoint is overkill and costlier, Async on p4d is wasteful for a tiny model, and a scheduled Batch Transform cannot serve interactive unpredictable requests.

question: A team is deciding between SageMaker Multi-Model Endpoints (MME) and Inference Components for hosting many models on shared GPUs. Which statements correctly distinguish them? (Select TWO.)
options: Inference Components support per-model autoscaling and independent compute allocation, whereas MME dynamically loads/unloads same-framework artifacts without per-model scaling policies
MME is well suited to a very large catalog of similar, individually low-traffic models loaded on demand from S3
Multi-Model Endpoints provide independent autoscaling for each hosted model
Inference Components require all models to share identical resource needs and a single scaling policy
Both options require a separate endpoint per model
explanation: Inference Components give each model its own compute footprint and autoscaling, while MME excels at large catalogs of similar, low-traffic models lazily loaded from S3 but without per-model scaling. MME does not offer independent per-model autoscaling, Inference Components do allow differing resource needs per component, and neither requires a separate endpoint per model.

question: An endpoint serving a 7B model with LMI shows acceptable median latency but very high tail latency and occasional out-of-memory errors during traffic bursts. The current config uses a large static batch size and waits to fill the batch. Which single change BEST reduces both tail latency and OOM risk?
options: Switch from static batching to continuous batching with a bounded max number of concurrent sequences and a max running-batch token budget
Increase the static batch size further to amortize per-request overhead
Raise the max_new_tokens limit so requests finish in fewer iterations
Disable tensor parallelism to free scheduling overhead
explanation: Static batching causes requests to wait for the batch to fill (tail latency) and can over-commit memory; continuous batching with a bounded concurrent-sequence and token budget admits requests dynamically and caps memory pressure, lowering tail latency and OOM risk. Larger static batches worsen waiting and OOM, raising max_new_tokens increases work, and disabling tensor parallelism reduces available GPU memory for the model.

question: A company runs a generative document-processing pipeline where each request can take up to 10 minutes and arrives in unpredictable bursts of tens of thousands. They want automatic queuing, scale-out under load, and scale-in to zero when the backlog clears to avoid paying for idle GPUs. Which SageMaker option natively provides this?
options: Asynchronous Inference, which queues requests, autoscales the backing instances on queue depth, and can scale to zero when the queue is empty
Real-time inference with a client-side retry queue
Serverless Inference with 10-minute timeouts
Batch Transform scheduled every minute
explanation: Asynchronous Inference has a built-in request queue, supports autoscaling on the ApproximateBacklogSizePerInstance metric, and can scale the fleet to zero when the queue drains, matching long, bursty jobs that should not pay for idle GPUs. Real-time has a 60-second timeout, Serverless cannot run 10-minute GPU jobs, and a per-minute Batch Transform is operationally clumsy and not queue-driven.

question: A team fine-tuned a Llama model with JumpStart and now wants to deploy it cost-effectively for moderate, steady real-time traffic that comfortably fits on one A10G GPU. They want the simplest reliable hosting with predictable latency. Which choice is BEST?
options: A single-model real-time endpoint on ml.g5.xlarge (A10G) with modest target-tracking autoscaling
A Multi-Model Endpoint even though only one model is served
Asynchronous Inference to queue the steady real-time requests
Batch Transform invoked continuously to emulate real-time
explanation: For one model with moderate steady real-time traffic that fits on an A10G, a single-model real-time endpoint on g5.xlarge with light autoscaling is the simplest, most predictable, and cost-appropriate option. MME adds needless complexity for a single model, Async introduces queuing latency unsuited to interactive traffic, and abusing Batch Transform for real-time is an anti-pattern.

question: An organization is selecting accelerator families for different generative workloads on SageMaker. Which recommendations are the BEST general-purpose fits? (Select THREE.)
options: g5 (A10G) for cost-effective real-time inference of small-to-mid models that fit in 24 GB per GPU
p4d/p5 (A100/H100) for hosting very large models requiring high GPU memory and bandwidth, or large-scale training
inf2 (Inferentia2) for cost-optimized, high-throughput inference after Neuron compilation
trn1 (Trainium) as the default choice for latency-critical single-request real-time inference
Serverless GPU inference for hosting 70B models with no instance management
explanation: g5/A10G suits cost-effective serving of smaller models, p4d/p5 (A100/H100) suits very large models and heavy training, and inf2/Inferentia2 targets cost-efficient high-throughput inference after Neuron compilation. Trainium is built for training rather than latency-critical single-request serving, and SageMaker Serverless does not offer GPU hosting for 70B models.

question: A team wants to optimize a JumpStart foundation model for faster, cheaper inference by applying techniques like speculative decoding, quantization, and compilation, packaged for deployment, without hand-building the optimization pipeline. Which SageMaker capability is designed for this?
options: SageMaker inference optimization toolkit (model optimization jobs) that applies quantization, speculative decoding, and compilation to produce an optimized deployable artifact
SageMaker Model Monitor data-quality jobs
SageMaker Feature Store online serving
SageMaker Clarify explainability jobs
explanation: SageMaker provides an inference optimization toolkit that applies quantization, speculative decoding, and compilation to foundation models to improve price-performance and outputs a deployable optimized artifact. Model Monitor, Feature Store, and Clarify address monitoring, feature serving, and explainability respectively, not inference acceleration.

question: A solution must keep an interactive 7B model warm 24/7 with sub-200 ms p99 latency, but the team also wants to cap cost. Traffic is steady during the day and a low but nonzero trickle at night. Which autoscaling configuration BEST balances the SLA and cost?
options: Target-tracking autoscaling with a minimum of one instance (never zero) to preserve warm capacity, scaling out during the day and in to the minimum at night
Scale to zero at night, accepting cold starts on the first nighttime request
Fixed provisioning at peak daytime capacity around the clock
Serverless Inference to avoid managing any minimum capacity
explanation: Because there is nonzero nighttime traffic and a strict latency SLA, a minimum of one warm instance preserves the p99 target while target-tracking scales out for daytime load and in at night to cap cost. Scale to zero would violate the SLA on the first nighttime request, fixed peak capacity overpays at night, and Serverless cannot host the 7B GPU model with this latency guarantee.

question: A team self-hosts a fine-tuned open-weights LLM on a SageMaker real-time endpoint and must enforce content safety policies on both inputs and outputs equivalent to a managed service. They do not want to build and maintain a custom moderation model. Which AWS approach BEST adds guardrails to a self-hosted SageMaker endpoint?
options: Invoke Amazon Bedrock Guardrails independently via the ApplyGuardrail API to screen prompts and completions around the SageMaker endpoint call
Enable a built-in Guardrails toggle on the SageMaker real-time endpoint configuration
Rely on the LMI container's native prompt-injection filter
Use SageMaker Model Monitor to block unsafe responses in real time
explanation: Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to any model, including self-hosted SageMaker endpoints, via the standalone ApplyGuardrail API to screen inputs and outputs without building a custom moderation model. SageMaker real-time endpoints have no built-in Guardrails toggle, the LMI container has no native injection filter, and Model Monitor detects drift offline rather than blocking responses inline.

question: A platform team must allow a microservice to invoke only two specific Anthropic Claude models in us-east-1, while explicitly preventing it from invoking any other foundation model or using cross-Region inference profiles. The IAM policy will be attached to the service role. Which design best enforces least privilege?
options: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the two specific foundation-model ARNs, and avoid using a wildcard Resource
Allow bedrock:* on Resource "*" but add a permissions boundary that denies bedrock:CreateModelCustomizationJob
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on Resource "*" with a condition aws:RequestedRegion equals us-east-1
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the two model ARNs plus a separate statement allowing the bedrock:InvokeModel action on all inference-profile ARNs in the account
explanation: Scoping the allowed actions to the exact foundation-model ARNs grants only what is needed and naturally excludes other models and inference profiles. A wildcard Resource with only a Region condition still permits every model in the Region, and adding an inference-profile statement would reintroduce cross-Region access the requirement forbids.

question: Your security team requires that an IAM role be permitted to call Bedrock only when the request originates from inside your VPC through an interface endpoint, and never from the public internet or another network. Which IAM policy condition most precisely enforces this for the InvokeModel action?
options: A Deny statement using NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp with your office CIDR ranges
An Allow statement with a condition on aws:SourceVpce matching the Bedrock interface VPC endpoint ID
An Allow statement with a condition on aws:PrincipalOrgID matching your organization
A condition on aws:SecureTransport set to true
explanation: The aws:SourceVpce condition key ties access to a specific interface VPC endpoint, guaranteeing traffic arrives through PrivateLink rather than the public endpoint. SourceIp filtering is brittle and does not prove the request used the endpoint, SecureTransport only enforces TLS, and PrincipalOrgID controls which org accounts can call, not the network path.

question: A regulated firm runs a Bedrock application in private subnets with no internet gateway or NAT. The app must invoke Bedrock models, read prompt templates from S3, and write invocation logs to S3, all without traffic leaving the AWS network. Which connectivity choices meet the requirement at the lowest ongoing cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Create an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 to handle both reads and log delivery
Add a NAT gateway and route 0.0.0.0/0 through it to reach the public Bedrock endpoint
Use a Bedrock gateway VPC endpoint, since Bedrock supports gateway endpoints like S3 and DynamoDB
explanation: Bedrock runtime is reachable only via an interface (PrivateLink) endpoint, while S3 supports a gateway endpoint that carries no hourly or per-GB charge, making it the cheapest private path to S3. An interface endpoint for S3 works but adds hourly and data-processing fees, a NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet, and Bedrock does not offer a gateway endpoint.

question: Compliance mandates that all data Bedrock stores or processes on your behalf, including model customization training data and the resulting custom model artifacts, be encrypted with keys your organization controls and can audit and revoke. What is the correct approach?
options: Rely on Bedrock's default AWS owned encryption, which already satisfies customer-managed key requirements
Encrypt the S3 training bucket with SSE-S3 and let Bedrock copy the data internally
Provide a customer managed AWS KMS key when creating the customization job and for the custom model, and grant Bedrock the necessary kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey permissions via the key policy
Use client-side encryption on the training files and pass the plaintext data key in the job request
explanation: Bedrock lets you supply a customer managed KMS key for customization jobs and custom models, which gives you key rotation, audit via CloudTrail, and the ability to revoke access. Default AWS owned keys are not auditable or revocable by you, SSE-S3 does not cover the model artifacts Bedrock produces, and passing plaintext data keys is insecure and unsupported.

question: A team has steady, predictable production traffic of roughly 40 requests per second to a single Claude model 24x7 and is hitting on-demand throughput throttling at peak. They want guaranteed throughput and the lowest cost for this sustained load. Which option is most appropriate?
options: Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a committed term for the model to reserve model units
Stay on on-demand and implement exponential backoff with jitter to absorb the throttling
Switch the workload to the Batch inference API to avoid throttling
Request a service quota increase for on-demand InvokeModel and keep paying per token
explanation: Provisioned Throughput reserves model units that guarantee a fixed throughput and, with a committed term, offers the lowest cost for steady high-volume workloads. Backoff and quota increases only mitigate on-demand throttling without guaranteeing capacity, and Batch is for asynchronous, latency-tolerant jobs, not real-time request/response traffic.

question: An analytics team needs to score 5 million customer reviews with a Bedrock model overnight. Latency per record does not matter, but total cost does. Which approach minimizes cost while completing the job?
options: Use the Bedrock Batch inference (CreateModelInvocationJob) API, which processes records asynchronously at a reduced per-token price
Use on-demand InvokeModel in a tight loop across hundreds of threads
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the night and tear it down in the morning
Use prompt caching on the on-demand endpoint to lower the per-record cost
explanation: Batch inference is designed for large asynchronous workloads and is billed at roughly half the on-demand token price, making it the cheapest option when latency is irrelevant. On-demand looping risks throttling and costs full price, Provisioned Throughput is billed by committed model-unit time and is overkill for a one-off job, and prompt caching helps only with repeated prompt prefixes, not unique reviews.

question: A chatbot sends a long, unchanging 8,000-token system prompt and tool definitions on every turn, followed by a short user message. Token costs from the repeated prefix dominate the bill. Which Bedrock capability reduces cost with the least application rework?
options: Enable prompt caching so the static prefix is cached and billed at a large discount on cache hits
Move the system prompt into a Knowledge Base so it is retrieved instead of sent
Switch to Provisioned Throughput to get a flat rate regardless of token count
Truncate the system prompt on every other request to halve input tokens
explanation: Prompt caching stores the repeated prefix so cache-read tokens are billed at a steep discount versus normal input tokens, directly targeting the cost of the unchanging prefix with minimal code changes. A Knowledge Base addresses dynamic retrieval not a fixed system prompt, Provisioned Throughput still meters work via model units, and truncating the prompt degrades behavior.

question: An auditor must be able to prove, for every Bedrock InvokeModel call over the last year, who made the call, when, and from where, AND separately review the actual prompt and completion content for a sampled subset. Which two configurations together satisfy both needs? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable CloudTrail data events for Bedrock to capture per-invocation API activity (identity, time, source)
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging, delivering request/response payloads to S3 (and/or CloudWatch Logs)
Rely on CloudTrail management events alone, which already log every InvokeModel request with payloads
Enable AWS Config rules to record the prompt and completion of each invocation
Turn on VPC Flow Logs to capture the prompt and completion content
explanation: CloudTrail data events record the per-call API activity (principal, time, source IP) but not payload bodies, while Bedrock model invocation logging captures the actual request and response content to S3/CloudWatch. Management events do not log InvokeModel or its payloads, Config records resource configuration not prompts, and Flow Logs capture network metadata only.

question: A team enabled CloudTrail data events for Bedrock across the organization and the monthly CloudTrail bill jumped sharply due to extremely high invocation volume. They still need an audit trail of management actions (model access changes, guardrail edits) but want to cut the data-event cost. What is the best action?
options: Disable Bedrock data events and keep management events, which are recorded at no additional CloudTrail charge
Delete the trail entirely to stop all charges
Switch data events to log only to CloudWatch Logs instead of S3 to avoid per-event billing
Reduce the S3 bucket lifecycle to delete CloudTrail logs after one day
explanation: CloudTrail charges per data event, but management events for one trail are delivered free, so disabling Bedrock data events while keeping management events preserves the audit of administrative actions at no extra charge. Deleting the trail loses all auditing, the destination does not change the per-data-event charge, and shortening retention does not reduce the per-event ingestion cost.

question: Under sudden load, an application receives intermittent ThrottlingException (HTTP 429) responses from Bedrock on-demand. The team wants maximum successful throughput without overwhelming the service or hammering it during outages. Which client behavior is the recommended best practice?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the request succeeds
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, capping the number of attempts
Catch the 429 and fail the request immediately so the caller can resubmit later
Open a new connection per retry to spread load across endpoints
explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries over time and prevents synchronized retry storms, which is AWS's recommended pattern for throttling. Tight-loop retries amplify the overload, failing immediately wastes recoverable requests, and opening new connections does not address the underlying rate limit.

question: A FinOps team wants to alert when a specific Bedrock model's token consumption spikes, so they can investigate runaway agents before the bill grows. Which CloudWatch metric, emitted by Bedrock, most directly supports this alarm?
options: Invocations and InputTokenCount / OutputTokenCount dimensions for the model in the AWS/Bedrock namespace
BillingEstimatedCharges in the AWS/Billing namespace filtered by model ARN
CPUUtilization for the Bedrock fleet
Number of items in the S3 invocation-log bucket
explanation: Bedrock publishes Invocations and token-count metrics (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount) to the AWS/Bedrock namespace per model, which is the direct signal for usage spikes. Billing alarms are coarse and not broken down by model ARN, there is no CPU metric exposed for the managed fleet, and counting S3 log objects is an indirect proxy that depends on logging being enabled.

question: You must compare two candidate models for a summarization use case using your own labeled reference summaries and quantitative metrics, with no human reviewers and a repeatable score. Which Bedrock feature fits best?
options: Bedrock model evaluation, automatic evaluation job using your custom prompt dataset and built-in metrics
Bedrock model evaluation, human evaluation job with an internal work team
Bedrock Guardrails configured with contextual grounding checks
A SageMaker Ground Truth labeling job
explanation: Automatic model evaluation runs algorithmic metrics against your dataset to produce repeatable, quantitative scores without human raters, exactly matching the requirement. Human evaluation introduces reviewers you explicitly want to avoid, Guardrails enforce policy at runtime rather than comparing models, and Ground Truth is for data labeling, not model scoring.

question: A legal team needs to judge model outputs for tone, helpfulness, and brand voice, which are subjective and not captured by automated metrics, using their own staff as reviewers. Which Bedrock capability should be used?
options: Bedrock model evaluation, human evaluation job using your own work team to rate responses
Bedrock model evaluation, automatic evaluation with the toxicity metric
Amazon A2I configured against the InvokeModel endpoint
CloudWatch anomaly detection on the OutputTokenCount metric
explanation: Human evaluation in Bedrock model evaluation lets you bring your own work team to rate responses on subjective dimensions, which automated metrics cannot capture. Automatic toxicity metrics measure only specific algorithmic properties, A2I is a general human-review service not integrated as a Bedrock evaluation job, and CloudWatch metrics describe usage, not output quality.

question: A security review requires that Bedrock model invocation logging be reliable and the log destination protected. Logging delivers request/response payloads to an S3 bucket and a CloudWatch log group. Which two configurations are required or strongly recommended? (Select TWO.)
options: Grant Bedrock a service role / resource policy permission to write to the chosen S3 bucket and CloudWatch log group
Enable SSE-KMS on the S3 bucket and grant the Bedrock logging principal access to the KMS key
Make the S3 logging bucket public so Bedrock can deliver logs without credentials
Disable bucket versioning to prevent Bedrock from creating duplicate log objects
Store logs only in CloudWatch because S3 cannot receive invocation payloads
explanation: Bedrock needs explicit write permission to the destinations, and if the bucket uses SSE-KMS the Bedrock logging principal must be granted use of the key or delivery fails. Public buckets are a serious risk and unnecessary, versioning is unrelated to duplicates, and S3 is a fully supported invocation-logging destination.

question: An organization wants central control so that only approved Bedrock foundation models can be used across all member accounts, regardless of individual account IAM policies. Which mechanism enforces this most effectively?
options: An AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) that denies bedrock:InvokeModel except on the approved model ARNs
An IAM permissions boundary applied manually in each account's roles
A resource-based policy on each foundation model restricting principals
A tag policy requiring an 'approved' tag on models
explanation: An SCP sets a permission ceiling across every account in the org and cannot be overridden by local IAM, making it the right central guardrail for restricting models. Permissions boundaries must be applied per-role and can be missed, foundation models do not expose customer-editable resource policies, and tag policies govern tagging conventions rather than enforce invocation restrictions.

question: A workload's traffic is bursty: long idle periods with occasional short, sharp spikes that briefly exceed on-demand limits. The team wants to avoid both throttling-induced failures and paying for idle reserved capacity. Which strategy balances cost and reliability best?
options: Use on-demand inference with exponential backoff plus a request queue to smooth spikes, and request quota increases if sustained limits are hit
Purchase the largest Provisioned Throughput commitment to cover the peak spikes
Run everything through Batch inference to eliminate spikes
Provision a small committed Provisioned Throughput tier sized to the peak and let it sit idle between spikes
explanation: On-demand with backoff and a smoothing queue charges only for tokens used and handles transient spikes, which fits bursty, mostly-idle traffic without paying for reserved capacity. Provisioned Throughput bills for committed model-unit time whether or not it is used, wasting money on idle periods, and Batch cannot serve interactive spike traffic.

question: A developer's IAM policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the model ARN, but calls fail with AccessDenied while the application also tries to use a customer managed KMS key to decrypt prompts stored in S3. The Bedrock action itself is permitted. What is the most likely missing permission?
options: The principal lacks kms:Decrypt on the customer managed key used to encrypt the S3 objects
The principal needs bedrock:CreateFoundationModel on the model ARN
The model ARN must be added to a security group
The KMS key must be an AWS managed key, not customer managed, for Bedrock to work
explanation: Reading SSE-KMS encrypted objects requires kms:Decrypt on the key in addition to S3 read and Bedrock permissions, and its absence produces AccessDenied even though InvokeModel is allowed. CreateFoundationModel is not a real customer action, security groups govern network not API authorization, and Bedrock fully supports customer managed KMS keys.

question: Token billing for Bedrock on-demand text models is based on which dimension, and what is the cost implication for a verbose application?
options: Input plus output tokens are billed, typically at different per-token rates, so reducing verbose outputs and trimming prompts both lower cost
Only the number of API calls is billed, so token length is irrelevant to cost
Only input tokens are billed, so long completions are free
A flat monthly fee per enabled model regardless of usage
explanation: On-demand text models bill for both input and output tokens, often at distinct rates with output usually more expensive, so controlling both prompt size and response length reduces spend. Billing is not per-call, output tokens are not free, and on-demand has no flat per-model fee.

question: A company must keep all Bedrock inference traffic private and prevent data exfiltration to non-approved AWS accounts or models even if a credential leaks. Which combination of controls best meets these goals? (Select THREE.)
options: An interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime with an endpoint policy restricting the allowed actions and model ARNs
An IAM identity-policy or SCP condition on aws:SourceVpce so credentials only work via the endpoint
Disabling Bedrock model invocation logging to reduce data stored
A VPC endpoint policy that allows only the organization's account IDs / approved model ARNs
Making the interface endpoint accessible from the public internet for redundancy
explanation: An interface endpoint with a restrictive endpoint policy, an aws:SourceVpce condition forcing all calls through that endpoint, and an endpoint policy limited to approved accounts/models together create private, exfiltration-resistant access. Disabling logging removes audit evidence without improving security, and exposing the endpoint publicly defeats the private-connectivity requirement.

question: A team commits to Provisioned Throughput for a base model. Mid-term they realize they actually need a fine-tuned custom version of that model with the same guaranteed throughput. What is the correct understanding of Provisioned Throughput here?
options: Provisioned Throughput can be purchased for custom (fine-tuned) models as well as base models, and is required to deploy a custom model for inference at guaranteed capacity
Provisioned Throughput applies only to base models; custom models must always run on-demand
Custom models are billed per API call with no throughput option
You must delete the custom model and re-import it as a base model to use Provisioned Throughput
explanation: Provisioned Throughput supports custom/fine-tuned models, and deploying a customized model for production inference generally requires purchasing model units for it. The claim that custom models run only on-demand or per-call is incorrect, and there is no need to convert a custom model into a base model.

question: Your finance team sees rising Bedrock costs and asks for per-team, per-application cost attribution within a single shared account. Which approach gives the most accurate breakdown?
options: Apply cost allocation tags to taggable Bedrock resources (e.g., provisioned models, evaluation/customization jobs) and use AWS Cost Explorer / CUR grouped by tag
Read the Invocations CloudWatch metric and multiply by a fixed assumed price
Split the total Bedrock line item evenly across all teams each month
Enable CloudTrail management events and count API calls per IAM user
explanation: Cost allocation tags surfaced in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report provide accurate, billing-grounded attribution for taggable Bedrock resources. Metric-times-assumed-price ignores per-token rate differences, even splits are inaccurate, and counting API calls does not reflect token-based pricing.

question: A new application is approved but InvokeModel calls fail because the account has never been granted access to the requested Claude model. What must an administrator do before invocation succeeds, and what permission governs it?
options: Request model access for that foundation model in the Bedrock console / via the appropriate API, an action gated by IAM permissions such as those for managing model access
Open a support case to AWS to physically provision GPUs in the account
Increase the on-demand token quota, which automatically enables the model
Attach the model's ARN to the VPC route table
explanation: Bedrock requires explicitly enabling access to specific foundation models for the account before they can be invoked, and that administrative step is itself controlled by IAM permissions. No GPU provisioning is involved, a quota increase does not grant model access, and route tables have nothing to do with model entitlement.

question: An incident requires correlating a suspicious Bedrock configuration change (a guardrail being disabled) with the identity that made it. Which CloudTrail event category captures this, and at what cost?
options: CloudTrail management events capture the guardrail configuration change and are recorded free for one trail per account
CloudTrail data events are required and are free of charge
Only Bedrock model invocation logging records guardrail changes
AWS Config is the only service that records who disabled the guardrail
explanation: Administrative/control-plane changes like disabling a guardrail are management events, which a single trail records at no additional charge along with the calling identity. Data events are billed per event and cover invocation-level activity, invocation logging stores payloads not config-change identity, and Config records resource state but management events directly capture the actor.

question: To minimize Bedrock spend without hurting user experience for an interactive assistant, which optimizations are sound? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable prompt caching for the large static instruction/context prefix reused across turns
Right-size the model, routing simple requests to a smaller/cheaper model and only escalating hard ones
Switch all interactive traffic to Batch inference for the lower token price
Disable streaming so output tokens are not billed
Always use the largest available model to reduce the number of retries
explanation: Prompt caching cuts the cost of repeated prefixes and model right-sizing avoids paying premium rates for easy queries, both lowering cost while preserving interactivity. Batch is asynchronous and unsuitable for live chat, streaming does not change token billing, and defaulting to the largest model raises cost rather than lowering it.

question: A multi-account organization wants member accounts to share a single set of Provisioned Throughput model units to avoid each buying its own commitment, while still centralizing the spend. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Centralize Bedrock inference in a shared services account that owns the Provisioned Throughput, and let member accounts invoke it via cross-account roles or a private endpoint
Buy separate Provisioned Throughput in every account so each is isolated
Use a single SCP to automatically pool unused model units across accounts
Enable Bedrock cross-account model unit sharing in the Organizations console
explanation: Provisioned Throughput is owned by the account that purchases it, so centralizing inference in a shared services account and granting cross-account/endpoint access lets teams share one commitment and consolidates spend. Buying per-account commitments fragments and wastes capacity, SCPs cannot pool capacity, and there is no Organizations feature that automatically shares model units.

question: A team wants to detect, in near real time, when a particular Bedrock model starts returning elevated client or server errors so they can fail over. Which is the most direct operational signal?
options: Create CloudWatch alarms on the InvocationClientErrors / InvocationServerErrors (and InvocationThrottles) metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace
Parse the S3 invocation logs hourly with Athena and alert on error strings
Poll CloudTrail every minute for failed InvokeModel events
Watch the Billing metric for a sudden drop in charges
explanation: Bedrock emits client-error, server-error, and throttle metrics to CloudWatch, so alarms on them give near-real-time error detection for failover. Athena over S3 logs is hourly and slow, CloudTrail polling is delayed and not designed for live alarms, and billing changes are a lagging, indirect indicator.

question: A data-privacy officer asks whether enabling Bedrock model invocation logging changes how Bedrock uses prompts and completions, and where the logged content resides. What is the accurate statement?
options: Invocation logging stores prompts/completions only in the customer's own S3 bucket and/or CloudWatch log group; it does not cause AWS to use that content to train base models
Enabling logging opts your data into base-model training
Logged content is stored in an AWS-owned account accessible to model providers
Logging automatically shares prompts with the foundation model provider for quality review
explanation: Invocation logs are delivered to the customer's own S3 bucket and/or CloudWatch log group, and Bedrock does not use customer prompts or completions to train base models. Logging is an audit feature, not a consent to training, and the content is not exposed to AWS-owned accounts or model providers.

question: Your application's per-account on-demand request and token-per-minute quotas for a model are consistently the binding constraint at peak, but traffic is steady all day. Comparing remedies, which is the most cost-effective long-term fix?
options: Move the steady high-volume portion to Provisioned Throughput, which provides guaranteed capacity independent of on-demand account quotas
Repeatedly request on-demand quota increases as traffic grows
Shard the workload across many IAM users to multiply the quotas
Add more retries with longer backoff to push more through the existing quota
explanation: For steady, high, predictable volume, Provisioned Throughput supplies guaranteed capacity decoupled from on-demand account quotas and is the durable, cost-effective fix. Quota increases are not guaranteed and lag growth, on-demand quotas are account/model-scoped so splitting across IAM users does not multiply them, and more backoff only slows requests without adding capacity.

question: An evaluation job must score models on a sensitive internal dataset that cannot leave a specific encrypted S3 location, and the results report must also be encrypted with the team's KMS key. When configuring a Bedrock model evaluation job, what should you ensure?
options: Reference the dataset in the approved S3 location, grant the evaluation service role read access and KMS decrypt, and specify the customer managed KMS key for the output results
Copy the dataset to a public bucket so the evaluation service can read it
Disable encryption on the output bucket because evaluation results are not sensitive
Embed the dataset inline in the job request to avoid using S3 at all
explanation: The evaluation job's service role needs read access and KMS decrypt for the source data, and you can specify a customer managed KMS key to encrypt the output, keeping sensitive data and results protected. Public buckets violate the constraint, disabling output encryption exposes results, and inline datasets are not how evaluation jobs ingest data.

question: Two teams debate IAM design: Team A proposes one broad role with bedrock:* used by all services; Team B proposes per-service roles each limited to specific actions and model ARNs with conditions. For a security-sensitive, audited environment, which is correct and why?
options: Team B, because per-service least-privilege roles limit blast radius, make CloudTrail attribution clear per service, and prevent unintended model or admin actions
Team A, because a single shared role simplifies CloudTrail since all activity appears under one identity
Team A, because bedrock:* is required for InvokeModel to function
Team B is wrong because IAM conditions cannot reference model ARNs
explanation: Distinct least-privilege roles scoped to required actions and model ARNs minimize blast radius and produce clear, per-service CloudTrail attribution, which is essential in an audited environment. A shared bedrock:* role grants far more than needed and muddies attribution, bedrock:* is not required for InvokeModel, and IAM resource ARNs/conditions do support scoping to specific models.
